133	## Category 3 — Moat Assessment (MOAT) — 4 items
134	
135	### `MOAT_01`
136	**Label:** All 6 canonical moat types evaluated
137	**Pass:** Every company in the landscape (plus `_startup`) has been assessed on all 6 canonical moat types (`network_effects`, `data_advantages`, `switching_costs`, `regulatory_barriers`, `cost_structure`, `brand_reputation`). `not_applicable` with evidence is acceptable.
138	**Fail:** One or more companies are missing moat assessments for canonical types. Incomplete coverage.
139	**Warn:** All companies assessed but some `not_applicable` ratings lack substantive evidence (<20 characters).
140	**Basis:** Completeness is non-negotiable for an investor-ready moat assessment. Skipping moat types suggests the analyst did not consider all dimensions of defensibility.
141	
142	### `MOAT_02`
143	**Label:** Moat evidence meets quality floor
144	**Pass:** All moats rated `strong` or `moderate` have evidence strings of 20+ characters that cite specific facts (not generic assertions).
145	**Fail:** Multiple `strong` or `moderate` ratings have empty or generic evidence ("Good moat", "Strong advantage"). `MOAT_WITHOUT_EVIDENCE` warnings present.
146	**Warn:** Most evidence is substantive but 1-2 entries are thin.
147	**Basis:** A moat rating without evidence is an opinion, not an assessment. Investors will challenge every moat claim — the evidence must be ready.
148	
149	### `MOAT_03`
150	**Label:** Trajectory included for each moat
151	**Pass:** Every moat assessment includes a trajectory (`building`, `stable`, `eroding`) with reasoning. Trajectory matches the evidence (e.g., growing user base + `building` for network effects).
152	**Fail:** Trajectories are missing or all set to `stable` without analysis (default-filling).
153	**Warn:** Trajectories present but reasoning is thin for some entries.
154	**Basis:** Moats are not static. Investors want to know which moats are strengthening and which are at risk. A `strong` moat that is `eroding` is very different from a `moderate` moat that is `building`.
155	
156	### `MOAT_04`
157	**Label:** Custom moats justified (if present)
158	**Pass:** Any custom moat dimensions (`custom_{slug}`) include a clear definition explaining why the canonical 6 types are insufficient, with evidence meeting the same quality floor as canonical moats.
159	**Fail:** Custom moats added without justification, or custom moat duplicates a canonical type (e.g., `custom_patents` when `regulatory_barriers` already covers it).
160	**Warn:** Custom moat is justified but evidence is thinner than canonical moat assessments.
161	**Basis:** Custom moats should be rare. Adding unnecessary custom dimensions dilutes the analysis. They must earn their place with a clear argument for why the canonical taxonomy is insufficient.
162

165	## Category 4 — Evidence Quality (EVID) — 4 items
166	
167	### `EVID_01`
168	**Label:** Per-competitor research depth recorded
169	**Pass:** Every competitor has a `research_depth` field (`full`, `partial`, or `founder_provided`) and `sourced_fields_count` in `landscape.json`. Provenance is transparent.
170	**Fail:** Research depth metadata is missing for most competitors. No way to assess evidence quality.
171	**Warn:** Research depth recorded for some competitors but not all.
172	**Basis:** Investors and the agent itself need to know how much of the analysis is researched vs. estimated. Provenance metadata enables honest qualification of claims.
173	
174	### `EVID_02`
175	**Label:** Majority of competitors have sourced evidence
176	**Pass:** 60%+ of competitors have `research_depth: "full"` (enriched via web research with multiple sourced fields).
177	**Fail:** Fewer than 40% of competitors have sourced evidence. Analysis is primarily based on agent knowledge or founder claims.
178	**Warn:** 40-60% of competitors have sourced evidence. Mixed research quality.
179	**Basis:** An analysis built primarily on agent knowledge (training data) is less reliable than one built on current research. Investors value current, sourced data.
180	**Mode gating:** None — EVID_02 is active in all input modes (deck, conversation, document). Only EVID_04 and NARR_03 are auto-gated; see the gating table above.
181	
182	### `EVID_03`
183	**Label:** Evidence sources distinguished (researched vs. estimated)
184	**Pass:** `evidence_source` fields are populated throughout positioning and moat data. Clear distinction between `researched`, `agent_estimate`, and `founder_override` provenance.
185	**Fail:** Evidence source fields are missing or all set to the same value (suggesting they were not genuinely tracked).
186	**Warn:** Evidence sources present but inconsistently applied (some entries have provenance, others do not).
187	**Basis:** Distinguishing researched facts from agent estimates is intellectual honesty. The report should make clear what is verified vs. inferred.
188	
189	### `EVID_04`
190	**Label:** Competitor financials/pricing sourced
191	**Pass:** For competitors where pricing or funding data is included, it has `evidence_source: "researched"` with specific sourcing (not just "agent knowledge").
192	**Fail:** Pricing/funding data is presented as fact but sourced from agent estimates. Stale or fabricated financial data.
193	**Warn:** Some financial data is sourced, some is estimated but labeled as such.
194	**Basis:** Competitor financials change frequently. Stale pricing data from training data is worse than no data — it creates false confidence.
195	**Mode gating:** Auto-gated to `not_applicable` in `deck` and `conversation` modes (these modes typically lack detailed competitor financials).

199	## Category 5 — Narrative Readiness (NARR) — 4 items
200	
201	### `NARR_01`
202	**Label:** Differentiation claims stress-tested
203	**Pass:** Every differentiation claim in `positioning.json` has been stress-tested with a `verifiable` assessment, `evidence`, and `challenge` (what an investor would push on). At least one claim has verdict `holds`.
204	**Fail:** No stress-testing performed, or all claims have verdict `does_not_hold`. The competitive narrative has no defensible differentiation.
205	**Warn:** Stress-testing performed but most claims are `partially_holds` — differentiation exists but is not strong.
206	**Basis:** Investors will push on every differentiation claim. The founder must know which claims hold up under scrutiny and which need qualification.
207	
208	### `NARR_02`
209	**Label:** Investor-ready competitive framing
210	**Pass:** The analysis frames competition constructively: acknowledges strong competitors without dismissing them, positions the startup's advantages clearly, and addresses "why will you win?" with evidence. Suitable for inclusion in an investor deck or data room.
211	**Fail:** Analysis is either dismissive of competitors ("they're not a real threat") or defeatist ("they're too far ahead"). Neither is investor-ready.
212	**Warn:** Framing is reasonable but could be stronger — some competitors are insufficiently analyzed or the "why we win" argument lacks evidence.
213	**Basis:** The output of this skill feeds directly into investor materials. The competitive narrative must be honest, evidence-backed, and constructive.
214	
215	### `NARR_03`
216	**Label:** Competition slide alignment (deck cross-check)
217	**Pass:** If a pitch deck was provided, the competitive analysis aligns with the competition slide. Discrepancies (competitors omitted from deck, different positioning claims) are flagged and explained.
218	**Fail:** Significant discrepancies between the deck's competition slide and the analysis, with no acknowledgment. Investor would see contradictions.
219	**Warn:** Minor discrepancies acknowledged (e.g., deck omits one competitor that the analysis includes) with reasonable explanation.
220	**Basis:** If the founder is using this analysis to improve their deck, the two must be consistent. An investor who sees the deck AND a competitive analysis expects alignment.
221	**Mode gating:** Auto-gated to `not_applicable` in `conversation` and `document` modes (no deck to cross-check).
222	
223	### `NARR_04`
224	**Label:** Defensibility roadmap articulated
225	**Pass:** Analysis includes a forward-looking view of which moats to build and in what order, based on current strengths and trajectory. Specific actions tied to moat-building.
226	**Fail:** No forward-looking defensibility discussion. Analysis is purely backward-looking (current state only).
227	**Warn:** Some forward-looking discussion but vague or not tied to specific moat dimensions.
228	**Basis:** Investors invest in trajectory, not just current state. A startup with `weak` moats but a clear, credible plan to build `moderate`+ moats is more attractive than one with no plan.
229

232	## Category 6 — Common Mistakes (MISS) — 3 items
233	
234	### `MISS_01`
235	**Label:** No "we have no competitors" claim
236	**Pass:** The analysis acknowledges competition honestly. Even in novel markets, alternatives (do-nothing, adjacent solutions) are identified.
237	**Fail:** The analysis concludes or implies "no real competitors" without substantiation. This is the single most common red flag VCs cite.
238	**Warn:** Competition is acknowledged but minimized ("they're not a serious threat" without evidence).
239	**Basis:** "We have no competitors" is the fastest way to lose investor credibility. Every product competes with alternatives — at minimum, the status quo. This check exists because the founder may push the agent toward this claim at Gate 1 or Gate 2.
240	
241	### `MISS_02`
242	**Label:** No vanity axes selected
243	**Pass:** Positioning axes were selected to reveal genuine competitive dynamics, not to make the startup look uniquely positioned. No vanity flags from `score_positioning.py`.
244	**Fail:** Both positioning axes are vanity — selected to put the startup alone in a quadrant rather than to reveal real market dynamics. The classic "we chose axes where only we score high."
245	**Warn:** One vanity axis detected. The map partially reveals dynamics but one axis is suspect.
246	**Basis:** The "vanity quadrant" (choose two axes where you score uniquely high and competitors cluster elsewhere) is the competitive positioning equivalent of an inflated TAM. Sophisticated investors see through it immediately.
247	
248	### `MISS_03`
249	**Label:** No feature-checkbox thinking
250	**Pass:** Competitive analysis focuses on dimensions that matter to buyers (speed, cost, outcomes, trust, switching effort) rather than feature checklists. Differentiation is expressed in terms of customer value.
251	**Fail:** Analysis is a feature comparison matrix ("we have X, they don't have X"). Features without buyer-value context. The classic "we have 12 features, they only have 8" thinking.
252	**Warn:** Mostly value-focused but some analysis sections devolve into feature comparisons.
253	**Basis:** Feature parity is a losing game — incumbents will copy features. Sustainable differentiation comes from structural advantages (moats), not feature lists. Investors care about defensible positioning, not feature counts.

## Differentiation Stress-Test

### Right-sized for 2-15 technician teams — not feature-bloated like enterprise tools

- **Verdict:** partially_holds
- **Verifiable:** Yes
- **Evidence:** The claim is true versus ServiceTitan ($245-$500/tech/month, 6-12 month implementation, mandatory annual contract) and FieldEdge (5-week mandatory onboarding, 8-50+ tech target). Both are genuinely enterprise-heavy and overbuilt for a 2-9 tech shop. However, Cadence's primary deal-stage competitors — Jobber and Housecall Pro — are themselves SMB-native platforms explicitly designed for the 1-15 tech segment. Jobber's positioning is 'affordable, easy field automation for small home service teams.' Housecall Pro is 'mobile-first FSM for small businesses and owner-operators.' The claim of 'not feature-bloated like enterprise tools' does not clearly differentiate from the platforms Cadence actually loses deals to. Source: Connecteam Jobber review 2026; FieldEx Jobber vs. HCP comparison 2026.
- **Investor Challenge:** Investors will ask: if Jobber and Housecall Pro are already right-sized for 2-15 tech teams, what specifically makes Cadence more right-sized? The claim needs to be sharpened to name a concrete bloat that exists in Jobber/HCP but is absent in Cadence — otherwise it only differentiates from enterprise tier, not from the actual competitive set the founder mentions.

### Faster onboarding than incumbent FSM platforms — no dedicated implementation required

- **Verdict:** partially_holds
- **Verifiable:** Yes
- **Evidence:** True versus ServiceTitan (6-12 months, $10K-$50K+ implementation) and FieldEdge (mandatory 5-week onboarding, $500-$2K setup). Both require dedicated implementation. However, Jobber is documented as self-serve with crews onboarded 'in a single afternoon.' Housecall Pro is described as quick-to-onboard with intuitive guided walkthroughs. Workiz offers 'hands-on and free onboarding, most accounts live in days.' The primary deal-stage incumbents (Jobber, HCP) already have self-serve onboarding without dedicated implementation. The claim differentiates against the wrong part of the competitive set. Source: McCary Group FSM small teams comparison 2026; Connecteam Jobber review 2026; UStech Automations HCP review 2026.
- **Investor Challenge:** Investors will note that Jobber and Housecall Pro — the platforms Cadence most often competes against in deals — are already self-serve with fast onboarding. 'No dedicated implementation required' is table stakes in the SMB FSM segment, not a differentiator. Cadence needs to quantify its speed advantage specifically vs. Jobber and HCP (e.g., 'live in 2 hours vs. 2 days') or reframe around a specific onboarding barrier those tools still carry.

### Scheduling and dispatch intelligence without the enterprise price tag

- **Verdict:** partially_holds
- **Verifiable:** Yes
- **Evidence:** ServiceTitan's Dispatch Pro (AI-powered assignment factoring skills, drive time, and job value) is the clearest example of enterprise-priced dispatch intelligence — at $245-$500/tech/month plus add-on costs. The gap between ServiceTitan's sophistication and what Jobber/HCP offer is real. However, Workiz ships Genius Scheduling (AI optimal slot suggestions based on tech availability, location, and schedule) and an AI Dispatcher as shipped features at $225-$325/month base — making this a partially occupied positioning. Cadence's claim of 'dispatch intelligence without the enterprise price tag' must account for Workiz, which already offers AI-level dispatch tools at SMB pricing. Source: Workiz route-planning features page; AppIntent.com AI dispatch software 2026 ranking.
- **Investor Challenge:** Workiz materially weakens this claim. Investors will ask: how does Cadence's dispatch intelligence differ from Workiz's Genius Scheduling and AI Dispatcher, given both target SMB pricing? Cadence needs either a clearer articulation of where its dispatch logic exceeds Workiz (e.g., multi-constraint optimization, vertical-specific routing rules, real-time reoptimization) or a repositioning that incorporates Workiz as a named competitor rather than treating this as an open gap.

## Coaching Commentary

Cadence scored 84.8% across the 25-item review — one point below the "strong" threshold of 85%, which is a meaningful distinction. "Solid" means the analysis is well-structured and investor-presentable, but two specific gaps are holding back the top grade, and both are fixable before the next investor conversation.

**What's working well.** Eighteen items passed outright. The competitive landscape is well-researched: Jobber, Housecall Pro, Workiz, ServiceTitan, and FieldEdge are all correctly identified and characterized. The stress-testing methodology is thorough — all three differentiation claims were assessed with evidence, specific investor challenges, and verdicts. The honest framing around strong competitors (Jobber's 100,000+ customers, ServiceTitan's post-IPO data position) is exactly what investors respect. Founders who pretend those players don't exist lose credibility in the room; you didn't.

**The two failures — both fixable before your next meeting.**

*COVER_03 — No emerging entrant addressed.* The landscape covers the established set well, but doesn't address the question investors will ask: "who's the AI-native startup coming for this market?" That could be a category answer ("no well-funded AI-FSM entrant has reached product-market fit in the 2-15 tech crew segment yet — here's why") or a named company you track. What it can't be is silence. If you genuinely believe no emerging threat is near-term relevant, say so with reasoning in your deck's competitive slide — a one-sentence statement with a rationale is all the criterion requires, and it shows you've done the thinking.

*NARR_04 — No defensibility roadmap.* This is the gap investors use to assess whether you've thought past the next 12 months. The moat scoring identified two moats in play: switching costs (weak) and cost structure (weak). Those are the starting points, not the endpoint. The roadmap question is: in what order do you invest in these, and what signals progress? A concrete version: switching costs are the lowest-cost upgrade from where Cadence sits today — every workflow integration, every imported historical dataset, and every team-specific configuration that customers build into the platform raises the cost of leaving. The milestone that signals this is working is retention at 12 months, not just at 3. Cost structure is a longer game and depends on scale; it's not the first moat to invest in at seed. Brand reputation and data advantages are absent today and expensive to build — they come after switching costs are established, not before.

**The three warnings — directional fixes.**

*POS_03 — 71% of coordinates are evidence-backed (target: 80%).* The two gaps are Cadence itself (scored by agent estimate, since there's no public product documentation yet at seed stage) and the manual-scheduling baseline. The manual-scheduling coordinate is inherently unresearchable, so that one is expected. For Cadence's own coordinates, the path to closing this gap is publishing something independently checkable — a pricing page, a feature comparison, case study quotes, anything that lets an outside researcher confirm where you sit on the axes you're claiming. This also makes investor due diligence easier, which compounds.

*NARR_01 — All three differentiation claims are "partially holds."* This is the most important of the three warns because it's structural, not presentational. The specific problem: the two claims that matter most to your target buyer (right-sized for 2-15 tech teams, faster onboarding) are also true of Jobber and Housecall Pro. They're your primary deal-stage competitors, not just your enterprise comparisons. That means you're not differentiated from the competitors a buyer would actually put you next to in an evaluation. The fix isn't to drop the claims — it's to sharpen them into something Jobber and HCP can't match. A few directions worth pressure-testing: dispatch intelligence that's native to the product (not an add-on), trade-specific workflow defaults that come pre-configured (not configured over time), or a specific onboarding guarantee that's quantified and backed. None of those are invented — they're directions the evidence here points toward. The sharpening work is yours.

*NARR_02 — Competitive framing honest but incomplete.* The framing correctly identifies gaps you can exploit: ServiceTitan's pricing, FieldEdge's onboarding friction, Workiz's AI add-on pricing. But the "why will you win?" answer is currently a set of exploitable weaknesses, not a positive claim about what makes Cadence the right choice. Investors want both. The Housecall Pro July 2026 trade-specific package launch is a live signal worth addressing directly — HCP is actively moving toward your segment, and acknowledging that move (and why it strengthens your position or what it means for your timing) is stronger than not mentioning it.

**On defensibility — context matters here.** Two moats identified, both weak — that's an overall defensibility grade of low. At seed stage, this is expected, not disqualifying. No seed-stage FSM startup has strong network effects or a data moat; those accrue over years of customer data and integrations. What investors are assessing at seed is whether you understand which moats you'll build and in what order, not whether they're already built. The roadmap item above (NARR_04) is your mechanism for answering that question. Switching costs are your most buildable near-term moat — invest there first, and make it visible in the narrative.

**One priority action.** If you're preparing for investor conversations in the next 30 days, the single highest-leverage fix is resolving the differentiation sharpening (NARR_01). Close the gap between "right-sized for small crews" and something Jobber and HCP can't claim — because until that's resolved, the NARR_02 framing and the NARR_04 roadmap both build on a foundation that won't hold under investor scrutiny. Get the positioning claim sharp, then build the roadmap and the framing from there.

Cadence scored 84.8% across the 25-item review — one point below the "strong" threshold of 85%, which is a meaningful distinction. "Solid" means the analysis is well-structured and investor-presentable, but two specific gaps are holding back the top grade, and both are fixable before the next investor conversation.

**What's working well.** Eighteen items passed outright. The competitive landscape is well-researched: Jobber, Housecall Pro, Workiz, ServiceTitan, and FieldEdge are all correctly identified and characterized. The stress-testing methodology is thorough — all three differentiation claims were assessed with evidence, specific investor challenges, and verdicts. The honest framing around strong competitors (Jobber's 100,000+ customers, ServiceTitan's post-IPO data position) is exactly what investors respect. Founders who pretend those players don't exist lose credibility in the room; you didn't.

**The two failures — both fixable before your next meeting.**

*COVER_03 — No emerging entrant addressed.* The landscape covers the established set well, but doesn't address the question investors will ask: "who's the AI-native startup coming for this market?" That could be a category answer ("no well-funded AI-FSM entrant has reached product-market fit in the 2-15 tech crew segment yet — here's why") or a named company you track. What it can't be is silence. If you genuinely believe no emerging threat is near-term relevant, say so with reasoning in your deck's competitive slide — a one-sentence statement with a rationale is all the criterion requires, and it shows you've done the thinking.

*NARR_04 — No defensibility roadmap.* This is the gap investors use to assess whether you've thought past the next 12 months. The moat scoring identified two moats in play: switching costs (weak) and cost structure (weak). Those are the starting points, not the endpoint. The roadmap question is: in what order do you invest in these, and what signals progress? A concrete version: switching costs are the lowest-cost upgrade from where Cadence sits today — every workflow integration, every imported historical dataset, and every team-specific configuration that customers build into the platform raises the cost of leaving. The milestone that signals this is working is retention at 12 months, not just at 3. Cost structure is a longer game and depends on scale; it's not the first moat to invest in at seed. Brand reputation and data advantages are absent today and expensive to build — they come after switching costs are established, not before.

**The three warnings — directional fixes.**

*POS_03 — 71% of coordinates are evidence-backed (target: 80%).* The two gaps are Cadence itself (scored by agent estimate, since there's no public product documentation yet at seed stage) and the manual-scheduling baseline. The manual-scheduling coordinate is inherently unresearchable, so that one is expected. For Cadence's own coordinates, the path to closing this gap is publishing something independently checkable — a pricing page, a feature comparison, case study quotes, anything that lets an outside researcher confirm where you sit on the axes you're claiming. This also makes investor due diligence easier, which compounds.

*NARR_01 — All three differentiation claims are "partially holds."* This is the most important of the three warns because it's structural, not presentational. The specific problem: the two claims that matter most to your target buyer (right-sized for 2-15 tech teams, faster onboarding) are also true of Jobber and Housecall Pro. They're your primary deal-stage competitors, not just your enterprise comparisons. That means you're not differentiated from the competitors a buyer would actually put you next to in an evaluation. The fix isn't to drop the claims — it's to sharpen them into something Jobber and HCP can't match. A few directions worth pressure-testing: dispatch intelligence that's native to the product (not an add-on), trade-specific workflow defaults that come pre-configured (not configured over time), or a specific onboarding guarantee that's quantified and backed. None of those are invented — they're directions the evidence here points toward. The sharpening work is yours.

*NARR_02 — Competitive framing honest but incomplete.* The framing correctly identifies gaps you can exploit: ServiceTitan's pricing, FieldEdge's onboarding friction, Workiz's AI add-on pricing. But the "why will you win?" answer is currently a set of exploitable weaknesses, not a positive claim about what makes Cadence the right choice. Investors want both. The Housecall Pro July 2026 trade-specific package launch is a live signal worth addressing directly — HCP is actively moving toward your segment, and acknowledging that move (and why it strengthens your position or what it means for your timing) is stronger than not mentioning it.

**On defensibility — context matters here.** Two moats identified, both weak — that's an overall defensibility grade of low. At seed stage, this is expected, not disqualifying. No seed-stage FSM startup has strong network effects or a data moat; those accrue over years of customer data and integrations. What investors are assessing at seed is whether you understand which moats you'll build and in what order, not whether they're already built. ## Differentiation Stress-Test

### Right-sized for 2-15 technician teams — not feature-bloated like enterprise tools

- **Verdict:** partially_holds
- **Verifiable:** Yes
- **Evidence:** The claim is true versus ServiceTitan ($245-$500/tech/month, 6-12 month implementation, mandatory annual contract) and FieldEdge (5-week mandatory onboarding, 8-50+ tech target). Both are genuinely enterprise-heavy and overbuilt for a 2-9 tech shop. However, Cadence's primary deal-stage competitors — Jobber and Housecall Pro — are themselves SMB-native platforms explicitly designed for the 1-15 tech segment. Jobber's positioning is 'affordable, easy field automation for small home service teams.' Housecall Pro is 'mobile-first FSM for small businesses and owner-operators.' The claim of 'not feature-bloated like enterprise tools' does not clearly differentiate from the platforms Cadence actually loses deals to. Source: Connecteam Jobber review 2026; FieldEx Jobber vs. HCP comparison 2026.
- **Investor Challenge:** Investors will ask: if Jobber and Housecall Pro are already right-sized for 2-15 tech teams, what specifically makes Cadence more right-sized? The claim needs to be sharpened to name a concrete bloat that exists in Jobber/HCP but is absent in Cadence — otherwise it only differentiates from enterprise tier, not from the actual competitive set the founder mentions.

### Faster onboarding than incumbent FSM platforms — no dedicated implementation required

- **Verdict:** partially_holds
- **Verifiable:** Yes
- **Evidence:** True versus ServiceTitan (6-12 months, $10K-$50K+ implementation) and FieldEdge (mandatory 5-week onboarding, $500-$2K setup). Both require dedicated implementation. However, Jobber is documented as self-serve with crews onboarded 'in a single afternoon.' Housecall Pro is described as quick-to-onboard with intuitive guided walkthroughs. Workiz offers 'hands-on and free onboarding, most accounts live in days.' The primary deal-stage incumbents (Jobber, HCP) already have self-serve onboarding without dedicated implementation. The claim differentiates against the wrong part of the competitive set. Source: McCary Group FSM small teams comparison 2026; Connecteam Jobber review 2026; UStech Automations HCP review 2026.
- **Investor Challenge:** Investors will note that Jobber and Housecall Pro — the platforms Cadence most often competes against in deals — are already self-serve with fast onboarding. 'No dedicated implementation required' is table stakes in the SMB FSM segment, not a differentiator. Cadence needs to quantify its speed advantage specifically vs. Jobber and HCP (e.g., 'live in 2 hours vs. 2 days') or reframe around a specific onboarding barrier those tools still carry.

### Scheduling and dispatch intelligence without the enterprise price tag

- **Verdict:** partially_holds
- **Verifiable:** Yes
- **Evidence:** ServiceTitan's Dispatch Pro (AI-powered assignment factoring skills, drive time, and job value) is the clearest example of enterprise-priced dispatch intelligence — at $245-$500/tech/month plus add-on costs. The gap between ServiceTitan's sophistication and what Jobber/HCP offer is real. However, Workiz ships Genius Scheduling (AI optimal slot suggestions based on tech availability, location, and schedule) and an AI Dispatcher as shipped features at $225-$325/month base — making this a partially occupied positioning. Cadence's claim of 'dispatch intelligence without the enterprise price tag' must account for Workiz, which already offers AI-level dispatch tools at SMB pricing. Source: Workiz route-planning features page; AppIntent.com AI dispatch software 2026 ranking.
- **Investor Challenge:** Workiz materially weakens this claim. Investors will ask: how does Cadence's dispatch intelligence differ from Workiz's Genius Scheduling and AI Dispatcher, given both target SMB pricing? Cadence needs either a clearer articulation of where its dispatch logic exceeds Workiz (e.g., multi-constraint optimization, vertical-specific routing rules, real-time reoptimization) or a repositioning that incorporates Workiz as a named competitor rather than treating this as an open gap.

## Differentiation Stress-Test

### Right-sized for 2-15 technician teams — not feature-bloated like enterprise tools

- **Verdict:** partially_holds
- **Verifiable:** Yes
- **Evidence:** The claim is true versus ServiceTitan ($245-$500/tech/month, 6-12 month implementation, mandatory annual contract) and FieldEdge (5-week mandatory onboarding, 8-50+ tech target). Both are genuinely enterprise-heavy and overbuilt for a 2-9 tech shop. However, Cadence's primary deal-stage competitors — Jobber and Housecall Pro — are themselves SMB-native platforms explicitly designed for the 1-15 tech segment. Jobber's positioning is 'affordable, easy field automation for small home service teams.' Housecall Pro is 'mobile-first FSM for small businesses and owner-operators.' The claim of 'not feature-bloated like enterprise tools' does not clearly differentiate from the platforms Cadence actually loses deals to. Source: Connecteam Jobber review 2026; FieldEx Jobber vs. HCP comparison 2026.
- **Investor Challenge:** Investors will ask: if Jobber and Housecall Pro are already right-sized for 2-15 tech teams, what specifically makes Cadence more right-sized? The claim needs to be sharpened to name a concrete bloat that exists in Jobber/HCP but is absent in Cadence — otherwise it only differentiates from enterprise tier, not from the actual competitive set the founder mentions.

### Faster onboarding than incumbent FSM platforms — no dedicated implementation required

- **Verdict:** partially_holds
- **Verifiable:** Yes
- **Evidence:** True versus ServiceTitan (6-12 months, $10K-$50K+ implementation) and FieldEdge (mandatory 5-week onboarding, $500-$2K setup). Both require dedicated implementation. However, Jobber is documented as self-serve with crews onboarded 'in a single afternoon.' Housecall Pro is described as quick-to-onboard with intuitive guided walkthroughs. Workiz offers 'hands-on and free onboarding, most accounts live in days.' The primary deal-stage incumbents (Jobber, HCP) already have self-serve onboarding without dedicated implementation. The claim differentiates against the wrong part of the competitive set. Source: McCary Group FSM small teams comparison 2026; Connecteam Jobber review 2026; UStech Automations HCP review 2026.
- **Investor Challenge:** Investors will note that Jobber and Housecall Pro — the platforms Cadence most often competes against in deals — are already self-serve with fast onboarding. 'No dedicated implementation required' is table stakes in the SMB FSM segment, not a differentiator. Cadence needs to quantify its speed advantage specifically vs. Jobber and HCP (e.g., 'live in 2 hours vs. 2 days') or reframe around a specific onboarding barrier those tools still carry.

### Scheduling and dispatch intelligence without the enterprise price tag

- **Verdict:** partially_holds
- **Verifiable:** Yes
- **Evidence:** ServiceTitan's Dispatch Pro (AI-powered assignment factoring skills, drive time, and job value) is the clearest example of enterprise-priced dispatch intelligence — at $245-$500/tech/month plus add-on costs. The gap between ServiceTitan's sophistication and what Jobber/HCP offer is real. However, Workiz ships Genius Scheduling (AI optimal slot suggestions based on tech availability, location, and schedule) and an AI Dispatcher as shipped features at $225-$325/month base — making this a partially occupied positioning. Cadence's claim of 'dispatch intelligence without the enterprise price tag' must account for Workiz, which already offers AI-level dispatch tools at SMB pricing. Source: Workiz route-planning features page; AppIntent.com AI dispatch software 2026 ranking.
- **Investor Challenge:** Workiz materially weakens this claim. Investors will ask: how does Cadence's dispatch intelligence differ from Workiz's Genius Scheduling and AI Dispatcher, given both target SMB pricing? Cadence needs either a clearer articulation of where its dispatch logic exceeds Workiz (e.g., multi-constraint optimization, vertical-specific routing rules, real-time reoptimization) or a repositioning that incorporates Workiz as a named competitor rather than treating this as an open gap.

## Coaching Commentary

Cadence scored 84.8% across the 25-item review — one point below the "strong" threshold of 85%, which is a meaningful distinction. "Solid" means the analysis is well-structured and investor-presentable, but two specific gaps are holding back the top grade, and both are fixable before the next investor conversation.

**What's working well.** Eighteen items passed outright. The competitive landscape is well-researched: Jobber, Housecall Pro, Workiz, ServiceTitan, and FieldEdge are all correctly identified and characterized. The stress-testing methodology is thorough — all three differentiation claims were assessed with evidence, specific investor challenges, and verdicts. The honest framing around strong competitors (Jobber's 100,000+ customers, ServiceTitan's post-IPO data position) is exactly what investors respect. Founders who pretend those players don't exist lose credibility in the room; you didn't.

**The two failures — both fixable before your next meeting.**

*COVER_03 — No emerging entrant addressed.* The landscape covers the established set well, but doesn't address the question investors will ask: "who's the AI-native startup coming for this market?" That could be a category answer ("no well-funded AI-FSM entrant has reached product-market fit in the 2-15 tech crew segment yet — here's why") or a named company you track. What it can't be is silence. If you genuinely believe no emerging threat is near-term relevant, say so with reasoning in your deck's competitive slide — a one-sentence statement with a rationale is all the criterion requires, and it shows you've done the thinking.

*NARR_04 — No defensibility roadmap.* This is the gap investors use to assess whether you've thought past the next 12 months. The moat scoring identified two moats in play: switching costs (weak) and cost structure (weak). Those are the starting points, not the endpoint. The roadmap question is: in what order do you invest in these, and what signals progress? A concrete version: switching costs are the lowest-cost upgrade from where Cadence sits today — every workflow integration, every imported historical dataset, and every team-specific configuration that customers build into the platform raises the cost of leaving. The milestone that signals this is working is retention at 12 months, not just at 3. Cost structure is a longer game and depends on scale; it's not the first moat to invest in at seed. Brand reputation and data advantages are absent today and expensive to build — they come after switching costs are established, not before.

**The three warnings — directional fixes.**

*POS_03 — 71% of coordinates are evidence-backed (target: 80%).* The two gaps are Cadence itself (scored by agent estimate, since there's no public product documentation yet at seed stage) and the manual-scheduling baseline. The manual-scheduling coordinate is inherently unresearchable, so that one is expected. For Cadence's own coordinates, the path to closing this gap is publishing something independently checkable — a pricing page, a feature comparison, case study quotes, anything that lets an outside researcher confirm where you sit on the axes you're claiming. This also makes investor due diligence easier, which compounds.

*NARR_01 — All three differentiation claims are "partially holds."* This is the most important of the three warns because it's structural, not presentational. The specific problem: the two claims that matter most to your target buyer (right-sized for 2-15 tech teams, faster onboarding) are also true of Jobber and Housecall Pro. They're your primary deal-stage competitors, not just your enterprise comparisons. That means you're not differentiated from the competitors a buyer would actually put you next to in an evaluation. The fix isn't to drop the claims — it's to sharpen them into something Jobber and HCP can't match. A few directions worth pressure-testing: dispatch intelligence that's native to the product (not an add-on), trade-specific workflow defaults that come pre-configured (not configured over time), or a specific onboarding guarantee that's quantified and backed. None of those are invented — they're directions the evidence here points toward. The sharpening work is yours.

*NARR_02 — Competitive framing honest but incomplete.* The framing correctly identifies gaps you can exploit: ServiceTitan's pricing, FieldEdge's onboarding friction, Workiz's AI add-on pricing. But the "why will you win?" answer is currently a set of exploitable weaknesses, not a positive claim about what makes Cadence the right choice. Investors want both. The Housecall Pro July 2026 trade-specific package launch is a live signal worth addressing directly — HCP is actively moving toward your segment, and acknowledging that move (and why it strengthens your position or what it means for your timing) is stronger than not mentioning it.

**On defensibility — context matters here.** Two moats identified, both weak — that's an overall defensibility grade of low. At seed stage, this is expected, not disqualifying. No seed-stage FSM startup has strong network effects or a data moat; those accrue over years of customer data and integrations. What investors are assessing at seed is whether you understand which moats you'll build and in what order, not whether they're already built. The roadmap item above (NARR_04) is your mechanism for answering that question. Switching costs are your most buildable near-term moat — invest there first, and make it visible in the narrative.

**One priority action.** If you're preparing for investor conversations in the next 30 days, the single highest-leverage fix is resolving the differentiation sharpening (NARR_01). Close the gap between "right-sized for small crews" and something Jobber and HCP can't claim — because until that's resolved, the NARR_02 framing and the NARR_04 roadmap both build on a foundation that won't hold under investor scrutiny. Get the positioning claim sharp, then build the roadmap and the framing from there.
